title: The Schleitheim Confession (Condensed)
subtitle: The Anabaptist charter of 1527 — seven articles on the believers' church, drafted around Michael Sattler months before his execution. The free-church idea, paid for in blood.
intro: In February 1527, Swiss and South German Anabaptist leaders met at Schleitheim, near the Swiss border, and agreed on seven articles — the movement's first confession. Their guiding figure, Michael Sattler, a former Benedictine prior, was arrested soon after; by May he had been tortured and executed, and his wife drowned days later. The confession they left sketches a church Christendom had not seen for a millennium: a voluntary congregation of confessing believers, marked off from the world by baptism and discipline rather than geography and birth, refusing the sword and the oath. Every side of the Reformation — Catholic, Lutheran, and Reformed — treated the vision as sedition and its holders as criminals. Readers of this platform's Baptist confessions are looking at those documents' bravest ancestor. The condensation below paraphrases the seven articles; it is not the full text.
text:
The following is a condensed summary of the seven articles. It is a faithful paraphrase, not the full text.

1. Baptism. Baptism is for those who have been taught repentance, believe their sins are taken away through Christ, and desire to walk in his resurrection — and who ask for it themselves. Infant baptism, the article says plainly, is excluded; the pope's practice finds no ground here. Baptism, in this vision, is the believer's own confession or it is nothing.

2. The ban. Those who have given themselves to the Lord and been baptized into one body, yet slip into error and sin, are to be warned privately, then before the congregation, and — if they will not turn — separated from the fellowship, according to the pattern of Matthew 18. Discipline replaces the magistrate: the church's only sword against sin among its members is exclusion from its table, aimed always at restoration.

3. Breaking of bread. The Lord's Supper is for the baptized — those united beforehand in the one body of Christ. Whoever has not been called by God out of the world's darkness into the light cannot share the one loaf, for the table presumes the fellowship it feeds.

4. Separation. The church is to be separated from the evil and wickedness the devil has planted in the world — from the works, ceremonies, and idolatry of a false religion made comfortable, and from the use of worldly force. Everything not united with Christ, the article argues, is the abomination to be shunned; the community's difference is its witness.

5. Shepherds. Each congregation is to have a shepherd of good report, who reads, exhorts, teaches, warns, disciplines, presides at the bread, and is supported by the congregation that called him. If he is driven off or martyred — the article assumes both are likely — another is to be ordained in the same hour, so that the flock is never left without its watchman.

6. The sword. Here Schleitheim goes further than any Reformation confession before or since. The sword — governmental force — is ordained of God outside the perfection of Christ: magistrates punish the wicked and protect the good, and this order is granted. But within Christ's community only the ban is used; Christians, following the one who refused to condemn the adulteress or seize a crown, do not wield the sword, go to war, or serve as magistrates. The Christian's weapons, the confession holds, are not carnal but spiritual.

7. The oath. Following the plain word of Jesus in the Sermon on the Mount, believers do not swear at all — their yes is yes, their no is no — for to swear by heaven or earth is to claim power over what only God commands.

annotations.note: The believers'-church principle in one clause: membership by personal confession, never by birth or civic status. Baptists a century later would build on exactly this foundation — which is why this document sits in this shelf's Baptist and Free Church group, upstream of 1644 and 1689.

annotations.phrase: ordained of God outside the perfection of Christ
annotations.note: Schleitheim's most radical and most debated move: the state is legitimate, but Christians do not staff it. Later Baptists parted company here — affirming magistracy as a lawful calling while keeping Schleitheim's demand that the state's sword never enforce the faith. Religious liberty in America descends from this argument, on both of its sides.

The article on shepherds legislates for martyrdom as an ordinary planning contingency — ordain the replacement the same hour. Within months Sattler was dead by the very courts the sixth article had granted legitimacy. No confession on this shelf was written closer to the fire.

The self-implication this platform will not skip: the magisterial reformers whose recoveries we celebrate approved the drowning and burning of the people who wrote this. Every tradition that now enjoys a free church owes a debt it spent a century collecting in blood.
